summary.case_overview: This landmark judgment of a 13-Judge Bench of the Supreme Court of India in Writ Petition (Civil) 135 of 1970 addresses the extent of Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 and the Constitutional validity of the Twenty-fourth, Twenty-fifth, and Twenty-ninth Amendment Acts [Page 1] [Page 2]. The Court evaluated whether the decision in I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab was correct and examined whether Parliament's amending power under Article 368 is plenary or limited by implied limitations or the basic structure of the Constitution [Page 2] [Page 6] [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 501]. The Court held that Golak Nath was incorrectly decided, ruled that Article 368 confers constituent power to amend any provision of the Constitution, but determined that the amending power does not extend to altering or destroying the basic structure or framework of the Constitution [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 484] [Page 501].
summary.facts_of_case: The petitioner, His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru, filed Writ Petition No. 135 of 1970 on March 21, 1970 under Article 32 of the Constitution to enforce fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 25, 26, and 31, challenging the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 as amended in 1969 [Page 1]. While the petition was pending, the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1971 was passed [Page 1]. Subsequently, Parliament enacted the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act on November 5, 1971, the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act on April 20, 1972, and the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act on June 9, 1972 [Page 2]. The Twenty-ninth Amendment placed the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Acts of 1969 and 1971 in the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution as items 65 and 66, protecting them from fundamental rights challenges [Page 2]. The petitioner amended the writ petition to challenge these Constitutional amendments [Page 2]. Given the grave Constitutional questions involved, the matter was referred to a larger 13-Judge Bench to determine the validity of the amendments and reconsider the decision in I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab [Page 2].
summary.legal_issues: The primary legal questions before the Court were: 1. What is the extent and scope of the amending power conferred on Parliament by Article 368 of the Constitution, and whether there are inherent or implied limitations on this power [Page 2] [Page 91] [Page 104] [Page 487]? 2. Was I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab correctly decided in holding that fundamental rights cannot be abridged or taken away by a Constitutional amendment and that an amendment under Article 368 is 'law' within the meaning of Article 13(2) [Page 2] [Page 6] [Page 484] [Page 501]? 3. Is the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971 constitutionally valid [Page 1] [Page 129] [Page 258] [Page 494] [Page 501]? 4. Are Section 2 and Section 3 (incorporating Article 31C) of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971 constitutionally valid [Page 1] [Page 194] [Page 258] [Page 361] [Page 374] [Page 495] [Page 498] [Page 501]? 5. Is the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972 constitutionally valid [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 500] [Page 502]?
summary.important_arguments_or_content: The petitioners contended that the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution under Article 368 is limited and does not empower Parliament to destroy or alter the basic structure, identity, or fundamental framework of the Constitution [Page 2] [Page 258] [Page 487] [Page 488]. They argued that fundamental rights are basic human freedoms that cannot be abrogated or taken away by Parliament, and that Article 31C destroys essential features of the Constitution, removes judicial review, and delegates amending power to State Legislatures [Page 2] [Page 487] [Page 496]. The respondents submitted that Article 368 confers an unrestricted and plenary constituent power on Parliament to amend any provision of the Constitution, including Part III [Page 2] [Page 91] [Page 104]. They argued that short of total repeal of the Constitution, Parliament can alter any provision, implement Directive Principles, and restructure the political or economic framework of the nation without implied or inherent limitations [Page 2] [Page 91] [Page 104] [Page 488].
summary.court_reasoning: The Court analyzed the distinction between ordinary legislative power and constituent power, holding that an amendment passed under Article 368 is made in exercise of constituent power and is not ordinary 'law' within the meaning of Article 13(2) [Page 129] [Page 485] [Page 486] [Page 501]. Consequently, the majority held that Golak Nath v. State of Punjab was wrong in holding that fundamental rights are immune from amendment [Page 484] [Page 501]. However, on the extent of the amending power under Article 368, the Court reasoned that while Parliament can amend any provision of the Constitution including fundamental rights, the word 'amendment' does not mean complete repeal or abrogation of the Constitution, nor does it authorize Parliament to alter, damage, or destroy the basic structure or essential framework of the Constitution [Page 258] [Page 361] [Page 374]. Regarding the 25th Amendment, the Court reasoned that replacing 'compensation' with 'amount' in Article 31(2) allows Parliament to fix payment that need not be a market-value equivalent, provided it is not illusory or arbitrary [Page 258] [Page 361] [Page 497] [Page 501]. Regarding Article 31C, the Court held that while laws enacted to give effect to Directive Principles in Article 39(b) and (c) can be granted protection, the final part of Article 31C which barred judicial review by making a legislative declaration conclusive was unconstitutional as it struck at the basic structure of the Constitution [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 500] [Page 501].
summary.decision_or_conclusion: The Court concluded that: 1. The majority decision in I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab holding that Parliament had no power to amend Fundamental Rights and that an amendment is 'law' under Article 13(2) was incorrect and was overruled [Page 484] [Page 501]. 2. Article 368 confers constituent power to amend any provision of the Constitution, but does not enable Parliament to alter or destroy the basic structure or framework of the Constitution [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 501]. 3. The Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971 is valid [Page 258] [Page 494] [Page 501]. 4. Section 2 of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971 is valid [Page 258] [Page 497] [Page 501]. 5. Section 3 of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971 (introducing Article 31C) is valid to the extent that it protects laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and (c), but the declaration clause ('and no law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to such policy shall be called in question in any court...') is unconstitutional and invalid [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 501] [Page 502]. 6. The Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972 is valid [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 500] [Page 502]. 7. The writ petitions were remitted to a Constitution Bench for determination in accordance with law [Page 374] [Page 502].

summary.simplified_explanation: In simple terms, this major decision by a 13-judge bench resolved a debate over whether Parliament can change any part of the Indian Constitution [Page 1] [Page 2]. The Supreme Court ruled that Parliament does have the power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, overruling an earlier decision (Golak Nath) that had barred amendments to fundamental rights [Page 258] [Page 484] [Page 501]. However, the Court established the 'Basic Structure Doctrine', holding that Parliament cannot use its amending power to destroy or alter the core identity or basic framework of the Constitution [Page 258] [Page 374]. The Court upheld the 24th Amendment, Section 2 of the 25th Amendment, and the 29th Amendment [Page 258] [Page 501] [Page 502]. It also upheld the main part of Article 31C (introduced by the 25th Amendment) which protects social welfare laws aimed at reducing wealth concentration, but struck down the portion of Article 31C that tried to stop courts from reviewing whether a law actually served that purpose [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 501] [Page 502].
